beats.narration_text: Yassou — Vedanshu here. Chapter nine adds two refinements to the retrieve stage. Re-rank what came back, and rewrite what you searched for. I built both against a real index and measured them. One of them did nothing at all, and finding out why is the whole video.

beats.act: problem — why a second pass exists at all
beats.narration_text: Here is the problem the whole chapter sits on. A fast retriever encodes your question and every document separately, into fixed vectors, and then compares numbers. That is what makes searching a huge index cheap. It also means a document's vector is computed without ever seeing your question. The two never look at each other.

props.headline: The Score Was Computed Before You Asked.
props.subline: A bi-encoder embeds every document once, with no query in sight, so retrieval is a lookup. The speed and the blind spot are the same design decision.

beats.role_note: Mandatory PROBLEM beat — the why that earns the build. No prompt yet.

beats.narration_text: So the ask is deliberately narrow. Keep the per-token vectors instead of pooling them away, score the query against each shortlisted chunk jointly, and time every pass. And prove the blind spot rather than asserting it: encode the same document beside two different questions and compare the bytes.

props.command: claude "write rerank.py — stage 1 embeds the corpus once and returns a top-5. stage 2 keeps per-token vectors and scores query against candidate jointly with MaxSim. time every pass, and prove a document's vector does not depend on the query."

beats.narration_text: Two functions carry the beat. MaxSim takes the query's token vectors and the document's, multiplies them into a similarity matrix, and for every query token keeps its single best match in that document. Unlike a pooled dot product, this score does not exist until a pair exists. The second function is the proof: same document, two questions, compare.

beats.act: cycle 1 · OUTPUT — the cascade, and what it costs
beats.narration_text: The run makes the asymmetry concrete. Stage one embeds twenty-eight chunks once, in about two and a half seconds, and every later query is one pass plus twenty-eight dot products. Stage two measured eighty-six milliseconds per query-document pair. On a shortlist of five that is fine. On a million chunks it is twenty-three hours, for one question.

props.headline: Cheap And Broad, Then Careful And Narrow.
props.costNote: 86 ms per pair is 428 ms on a 5-chunk shortlist — and 23.8 hours per query across a million chunks. That gap is the only reason the second stage is affordable.
props.caption: Redrawn from the chapter's Fig. 01, carrying this reel's own measured timings. Stage 2 here is late interaction, not a cross-encoder — see the summary.
props.citation: two-stage framing: Ch. 9; bi-encoder speedup after Reimers & Gurevych, 2019

beats.act: cycle 1 · OUTPUT — the result, which is a null
beats.narration_text: And then the result. Across six questions the re-ranker promoted nothing and demoted nothing. Here is the sharpest one. It did reorder — look at the lines cross. But the document that actually answers this question is not in either column. It never made the top five, so stage two never saw it. It reordered the wrong five.

props.headline: It Reordered. The Wrong Five.
props.sparkLine: Stage 2 only sees what stage 1 sent.
props.query: When am I allowed to change my health plan?
props.verdict: Across all six questions: 0 promoted, 0 demoted.
props.missing: OE-300 — Open Enrolment Window — is the document that answers this question. It was never in the top-5, so no re-ranker could reach it.
props.caption: Measured by this reel's own rerank.py over six questions. Ranks are document-level: any chunk of the right document counts.
props.citation: Ch. 9 §“Re-ranking”; re-ranking as post-retrieval after Gao et al., 2023/2024

beats.act: summary — the lesson, and the limits of this test
beats.narration_text: So: the expensive second pass is real, and on this corpus it moved nothing. Zero promoted, zero demoted. Because a re-ranker reorders a shortlist — it cannot retrieve. Whatever the first pass missed, the second pass never sees. Two honest limits. Six questions is a small test, and my second stage is late interaction, not the cross-encoder the chapter describes. A real one might well have moved things.

props.headline: Stage one sets the ceiling.
props.subline: A re-ranker can only reorder the shortlist it was handed, so whatever the first pass missed it never sees. Measured on six questions, with a stand-in re-ranker — not the cross-encoder the chapter describes.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: take the last fifty questions my RAG system answered, and for each one report whether the answering document was in the first-pass shortlist at all. Then split them — the ones where it was present but ranked low, and the ones where it was missing entirely. Run that before you add a re-ranker. The first group is what re-ranking can fix. The second group is not, and if that is most of them, a re-ranker is the wrong purchase.
